The prolonged incubation period of the Sooty shearwater (Ardenna grisea) is a defining feature of its early life history, reflecting the slow developmental pace typical of many Procellariiformes. Eggs are incubated at a mean temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], and under these conditions, hatching occurs after approximately 56 days [ab = approximately 56 days]. The newly emerged chick is relatively heavy, with a wet weight at birth measured at 113 grams [Wwb = 113 grams]. This substantial initial mass is supported by a large yolk reserve and is an adaptation to the long intervals between parental provisioning trips, which can span several days as adults forage over vast distances in the Southern Ocean. The chick's early development is thus buffered against the uncertainty of food delivery, allowing it to endure periods without feeding while still investing energy in tissue growth and thermoregulation.

Once hatched, the nestling enters a phase of rapid mass accumulation, fueled by frequent feeds of lipid-rich stomach oil and partially digested prey delivered by both parents. Under the thermal conditions typical of an actively metabolizing chick, approximately 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the young bird reaches its ultimate wet weight prior to fledging at 950 grams [Wwi = 950 grams], a value that substantially exceeds the mean adult mass of around 740 grams reported for breeding individuals in AnAge. This surplus mass is critical: it provides an energetic buffer during the challenging post-fledging period when the juvenile must learn to forage independently without parental assistance. The peak mass is attained after a protracted nestling period, which contrasts sharply with the shorter developmental schedules observed in smaller, less pelagic seabird species.

The transition to independence is marked by a specific developmental milestone known as fledging, which in this species occurs at 195 days after hatching [tx = 195 days after hatching] at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This extended duration in the nest, measured at a body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], reflects the considerable time required for the full development of flight feathers and the accumulation of the necessary body reserves for sustained flight over the open ocean. Following nest departure, the fledgling embarks on a long period of pelagic wandering, during which it refines its hunting skills. This pre-reproductive phase ultimately culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity, a life-history event that does not occur until significantly later in the bird's life.

The overall life-history strategy of Ardenna grisea is characterized by a very slow pace of life, with a single egg laid per breeding attempt. This combination of delayed maturation, low fecundity, and extended lifespan makes the Sooty shearwater highly vulnerable to anthropogenic threats such as bycatch and climate-driven shifts in prey availability, as population recovery from any decline is necessarily a multi-decadal process.
